ai_text_indicator.disclaimer: Advisory only, not an academic-integrity determination. This is a stylometric heuristic over surface features (sentence-length uniformity, lexical diversity, transition-phrase density, opening-word repetition, and sentence-embedding self-similarity) -- it cannot verify authorship and cannot detect real generative-model watermarks (e.g. Google SynthID), which are cryptographic signals embedded at the token-sampling level and are not recoverable from output text by any third party without the issuing model's own detection service. Formal academic prose already exhibits many of these same surface features, so well-written human capstone chapters can score in the 40-60 range; this indicator must never be used to block a submission or as a plagiarism/integrity charge on its own.

sections_analyzed: scope and limitations of the study

manuscript_sections.name: introduction
manuscript_sections.text:
Research writing influences the research competency and academic preparedness of the student researchers during their academic courses, and at the same time puts an evaluative burden on the advisers and the panelists who evaluate the quality of each research manuscript. Despite the apparent improvements, research writing can still suffer from generic and logical problems in terms of objectives that stray from problem statements and conclusions that lack support from survey and validation evidence, which tend to be undetected until the end of writing (Xue, 2024).
The real challenge for the students is that they typically don't realize that their objectives no longer align with their problem statement, or that their results don't have the data backing until it is time for consultation or defense, when it costs much more to fix the manuscript. The burden is the same for advisers and panelists: Manual, section-by-section review is time-consuming and expensive to ensure that each section of a manuscript is reviewed properly, particularly when dealing with high advising loads and increasing submission volumes that have been demonstrated to reduce review quality (Thakkar et al., 2025).
To address these review challenges, the research team proposes Resync, an AI-powered system that uses natural language processing to evaluate the coherence and consistency of research manuscripts. The system compares the uploaded manuscript to the corresponding template to determine where the manuscript should include sections, it then analyzes the manuscript overall to determine the areas of logical and coherence gaps in the manuscript and displays a Coherence Score, an Overall Assessment and the Recommendations to correct the detected gaps. Resync is designed to ensure that the logical and evidentiary consistency is validated for a research manuscript.
Resync is intended to be beneficial for all those who engage in the research process. Student researchers are able to identify inconsistencies earlier in the process, before consultation or submission, thereby cutting down revision cycles. Advisers have more time to spend on substance, and less time on manual checks. Panelists are able to walk into a defense with manuscripts that have already undergone AI-assisted coherence checking, allowing them to focus their evaluation on the depth and quality of the research rather than flagging basic inconsistencies. All these benefits help to build stronger and more defensible research outcomes.

manuscript_sections.name: rationale of the study
manuscript_sections.text:
This research is motivated by the challenging nature of manually verifying, checking, and aligning complex, non-linear relationships among multiple chapters of a research manuscript (Kashyap et al., 2023). Traditional manual, line-by-line checking often misses out on capturing key issues of inconsistency and weak correlation across sections early in the writing process (Tan & D'Souza, 2026).  This diagnostic failure may lead student drafts to be susceptible to logical inconsistencies that could not be detected, including research objectives that are not aligned with the main problem statement and conclusions that are based on research findings, but not on empirical data (Xue, 2024). Hence, the high volume of manual and repetitive reviews causes high cognitive load and acute mental fatigue for the adviser and panelists to evaluate these documents within tight institutional deadlines (Chikhi et al., 2022; Kunasegaran et al., 2023). A delayed and systematic anomaly detection process causes student writing communities to be stuck in inefficient writing routines, resulting in high manuscript rejection rates and delayed corrective measures (Ngo et al., 2022).
Resync, the proposed study, directly seeks to solve these operational inefficiencies, supporting manual review processes that are slow and subjective with a consistent, AI-assisted digital workspace. The system uses natural language processing to assess the coherence of a manuscript, comparing its sections against one another to identify logical inconsistencies early.
Current automated writing evaluation (AWE) tools have barely considered macro-level structural coherence and have concentrated on micro-level mechanics such as grammar (Xue, 2024; Rahimi et al., 2024). Resync is designed to solve this problem by resolving macro-level dependencies which significantly decreases review turnaround times, speeds up draft progress, and brings back review quality under heavy advising loads (Fleckenstein et al., 2023; Thakkar et al., 2025). This systematic pre-screening process frees up the time and cognitive load of faculty members who are supposed to review manuscripts so that they can focus on substantive rather than repetitive logical checks, and provides a consistent view of manuscript consistency to defense panelists (Chikhi et al., 2022; Thakkar et al., 2025).
In addition to the time saving, implementing Resync directly addresses the actual cost savings from the traditional, paper-based drafting and feedback process. Student researchers are burdened with numerous expenses, especially in resource-poor regional higher education centers such as Cebu, where they must print their paper drafts several times to get them reviewed manually. Logical inconsistencies between sections often force students to repeatedly print and revise their papers, as these inconsistencies go undocumented until the final oral defense, which is both costly and time-consuming (Trinidad et al., 2025). The Resync feature removes this material waste as a digital ‘pre-submission’ check point. The system validates the manuscript's overall consistency before printing, helping researchers catch coherence issues that could otherwise go undetected until later stages, reducing the financial resources wasted on premature printing (Kashyap et al., 2023). This automated pre-screening process helps student researchers economically and streamlines the research writing process.
The study is crucial for educational and institutional institutions that are looking for digital transformation. The continued disparity in the output and the assessment of the quality of research work carried out by the students at the local universities and the assessment done by the institutions seriously restricts the capacity of the local universities to produce rigorous, consistent and high quality research output (Da Silva, 2022 and Ngo et al., 2022). Traditional administrative reviews are lacking in timely and coordinated support, leaving thesis revision cycles long and student graduation delays (Hesselberg et al., 2023; Trinidad et al., 2025). By providing a localized, context-aware digital system that delivers real-time structural diagnostics and automated revision recommendations, Resync bridges the gap between student writing practices and formal institutional standards. Furthermore, by documenting the system's performance and design boundaries, this study serves as a vital methodological model for future researchers and developers seeking to design context-aware educational technologies.

manuscript_sections.name: objectives of the study
scope and limitations of the study
manuscript_sections.text:
This study covers the development and implementation of Resync, a web and mobile platform that uses natural language processing to evaluate the logical flow and coherence of research manuscripts. Researchers submit their manuscripts through publicly shared Google Docs links or direct file uploads. The system accepts English-language, single-column, text-based research manuscripts submitted through either method. Resync correlates content across the sections of a manuscript to detect contextual and logical inconsistencies, and evaluates how each citation is used and referenced throughout the manuscript. For external references, the system checks only whether the cited source exists and is publicly accessible; sources that are inaccessible or unavailable are flagged accordingly. Resync generates a Coherence Score, an Overall Assessment of the manuscript's logical consistency, and explainable AI-supported suggestions to guide researchers in addressing identified inconsistencies. Its outputs serve as decision-support tools, with the final interpretation and evaluation remaining the responsibility of the adviser or panelist. The findings aim to reflect broader academic conditions, as research manuscript inconsistencies are a common concern across higher education institutions in the Philippines.
This study does not assess Resync's effect on defense outcomes or panel scores, or changes in researchers' writing behavior over time. The system requires a stable internet connection, and the quality of that connection directly affects the speed and reliability of document processing and result generation. It accepts submissions only as publicly shared Google Docs links or uploaded document files and does not process handwritten manuscripts, image-only or scanned files, multi-column layouts, or private files. Citation validation is limited to checking whether a source is publicly accessible, and while the system attempts to verify the existence and accessibility of cited references through public sources, results are not guaranteed to be fully accurate, as AI systems may inconsistently identify or interpret citation accessibility. Accuracy may vary with a document's clarity and formatting. Resync detects inconsistencies in how the sections of a manuscript correlate and align with one another, and does not perform plagiarism checking or verify the factual accuracy of the claims, data, or content presented in the manuscript. Institutional adoption, integration with university grading systems, and factors such as digital literacy or device availability are outside the scope of this study.
Significance of the Study
The study brings multiple benefits to various stakeholders involved in or affected by the development and implementation of Resync.
Student Researchers. Students taking up thesis or capstone manuscript research will be the main beneficiaries. Resync's cross-section document analysis, AI-driven coherence evaluation, and automated inconsistency reporting will support researchers in reviewing their own work. This will help identify logical and coherence issues in the manuscript early, allowing researchers to make timely, informed decisions when revising their work.
Advisers. Capstone advisers will benefit from Resync without directly using the system themselves. Because researchers can address inconsistencies before consultations using Resync, advisers receive more coherent and logically consistent manuscripts, allowing them to focus their time on providing deeper academic guidance rather than identifying inconsistencies and logical issues.
Panelists. Defense panelists will also be able to benefit from Resync, but not as users of the system. By the time the manuscripts they review have been AI-assisted coherence evaluated by the researcher using Resync, they will be more coherent, consistent and defensible. This enables the panelist(s) to have a more streamlined and targeted evaluation at the defence.
Academic Institutions. Although not the direct daily users of the "Resync", higher education institutions will benefit from its indirect effects on research production. The platform supports the improvement of research output quality in institutional databases or local libraries with well-structured and well-drafted research outputs.
Researchers. The researchers developing the “Resync” will have valuable experience and skills to help both their academic and professional development. It places the researchers in a position to be partners of technological innovation in educational technology and to be the advocates of the application of digital tools in the management of institutional research.
Future Researchers. The study offers valuable insights and methodologies that can be used by researchers and developers in the field of educational technology and Natural Language Processing (NLP). It will stimulate new development of integrated tools for logical coherence analysis, cross-section document validation, and academic checking for specific sections.
Flow of the Study
This diagram below shows the study's different inputs, processes, and outputs. The procedure involves submitting research manuscripts through publicly shared Google Docs links or file upload, correlating content across sections to detect contextual and logical inconsistencies, and formulating a Coherence Score to achieve the desired outcome.

The process phase follows the Agile Methodology, which includes the stages of planning, requirement analysis, designing, development, testing, deployment and review. During these stages, the system is developed and refined to analyze research manuscripts, correlate content across sections, detect contextual and logical inconsistencies, and formulate coherence assessments.
The output phase is the development of Resync: An AI-Powered Research Manuscript Coherence and Inconsistency Detection System. The system provides automated manuscript analysis, detects contextual and logical inconsistencies across manuscript sections, formulates a Coherence Score based on cross-section correlation, and offers recommendations supported by explainable AI to guide researchers in improving the logical consistency of their research manuscripts.
Definition of Terms
Capstone Adviser. This refers to the faculty member assigned to guide and supervise student researchers throughout the development of their capstone manuscript.
Citation Validation. This refers to the process of verifying whether the references cited in a research manuscript are publicly accessible. The proposed system checks only publicly available references and notifies users when a cited source cannot be accessed.
Coherence Score. This refers to the numerical score generated by Resync that indicates the overall coherence of a research manuscript after comparing its sections and its manuscript template.
Correlation. This refers to the degree to which ideas, concepts, and content across different sections of a research manuscript relate to and support one another. In this study, Resync evaluates correlation by comparing the content of each section against the structure and expected content defined in the manuscript template, forming the basis for the Coherence Score.
Decision-Support Output. This refers to the Coherence Score, Overall Assessment, inconsistency reports, and recommendations generated by Resync. These outputs are intended to assist, rather than replace, the judgment of advisers and panelists during manuscript evaluation.
Explainable AI (XAI). This refers to a set of artificial intelligence methods and techniques that make a model's outputs and decision-making processes interpretable to human users. In this study, Explainable AI serves as the operational framework for generating Resync's diagnostic reports, ensuring that each flagged inconsistency is not an unexplained output but is instead accompanied by transparent justifications specifically detailing what the logical gap is, why it violates structural coherence, and providing an actionable recommendation to fix the draft.
Inconsistency Detection. This refers to the feature of Resync that identifies contradictions, redundancies, irrelevant content, and other inconsistencies within a manuscript or between the manuscript and its manuscript template.
Inconsistency Report. This refers to the system-generated report that presents the inconsistencies identified during manuscript analysis, including issues related to coherence, redundancy, relevance, and reference accessibility.
Manuscript Template. This refers to the structural format required by a researcher's institution for organizing a capstone manuscript, including the required chapters and sections. Within the proposed system, researchers may upload their manuscript template so that Resync can reference the expected content of each section and correlate ideas across the manuscript accordingly.
Natural Language Processing (NLP). This refers to a branch of artificial intelligence that enables computers to process, understand, and analyze human language. In this study, NLP is used by Resync to analyze research manuscripts and compare them with its manuscript template.
Overall Assessment. This refers to the summary evaluation generated by Resync after analyzing the research manuscript. It provides an overall interpretation of the manuscript's coherence and consistency based on the system's analysis.
Panelist. This refers to a faculty member or expert assigned to evaluate the validity, coherence, consistency, and overall quality of a capstone manuscript during its oral defense.
Recommendation Generation. This refers to the feature of Resync that produces recommendations based on the inconsistencies detected during manuscript analysis. These recommendations are intended to guide student researchers in improving the coherence and consistency of their manuscripts.
Researcher. This refers to the primary user of Resync — an individual who submits a research manuscript for analysis. Researchers upload their manuscript along with its corresponding manuscript template, allowing the system to correlate content across sections, detect inconsistencies, and generate a Coherence Score, Overall Assessment, and recommendations to guide them in revising their work
Research Manuscript. This refers to the written research output submitted by student researchers as a requirement for their degree program. It consists of interconnected sections, including the title, statement of the problem, objectives, methodology, findings, conclusions, and other supporting documents analyzed by the proposed system.
Resync. This refers to the AI-powered Research Manuscript Coherence and Inconsistency Detection System developed in this study. It analyzes a research manuscript against its manuscript template to evaluate the correlation of content across sections, detect inconsistencies, verify publicly accessible references, generate a Coherence Score and Overall Assessment, and provide recommendations for manuscript improvement.
Sections. Refer to the distinct parts that comprise a research manuscript, such as the introduction, review of related literature, methodology, results and discussion, and conclusion. In the context of Resync, sections serve as the primary units of analysis through which the system evaluates the logical consistency and coherence of the manuscript by correlating content across each part.

manuscript_sections.name: theoretical background
manuscript_sections.text:
This study is anchored to the Information Processing Theory, introduced by George Miller in 1956, which describes how both humans and machines receive, process, store, and retrieve information in a structured and systematic manner. The theory likens the cognitive process to a computer system, wherein incoming data is encoded, processed through a series of operations, and stored for future retrieval and use. In the context of Resync, this theory provides the foundational basis for how the system receives submitted research manuscripts as input, processes their textual content through natural language processing, compares sections for correlation and consistency, and retrieves structured outputs in the form of an Coherence Score, Overall Assessment, and Recommendations. Miller (1956) asserts that information must pass through a series of processing stages before it can be meaningfully interpreted and acted upon. For Resync, these stages mirror the system's pipeline of document intake, NLP-based comparison, inconsistency detection, and report generation, ensuring that manuscript evaluation is performed systematically and objectively rather than relying solely on manual human review. This shift in computational processing is particularly vital because human evaluators often face cognitive constraints and mental fatigue when manually reviewing lengthy manuscripts for extended periods (Chikhi et al., 2022; Kunasegaran et al., 2023).
Supporting the Information Processing Theory, the Constructivist Theory, developed by Jean Piaget and later expanded by Lev Vygotsky, suggests that learners actively construct knowledge and improve their understanding through experience, reflection, and meaningful feedback. Vygotskian constructivism and his concept of the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) further emphasize that learners benefit most when they receive guided support that bridges the gap between what they currently know and what they are capable of achieving. In relation to Resync, this theory justifies the system's Inconsistency Report and Recommendations output, which serves as a structured feedback mechanism for student researchers. Rather than simply flagging errors, Resync provides actionable guidance that encourages students to reflect on their manuscript's weaknesses and actively revise their work before final submission or oral defense. Constructivism adds an educational layer to the system's purpose by explaining how students' engagement with automated feedback can lead to meaningful improvement in research quality and writing consistency. This is supported by contemporary educational research, which demonstrates that structured rubrics function as evaluative support that significantly enhance student writing quality, academic performance, and self-efficacy (Panadero et al., 2023; Chen & Gong, 2025).
Another theory that supports the proposed system is the Automation Theory, which explains how repetitive, rule-based, and time-consuming human tasks can be systematically delegated to machines to achieve faster, more consistent, and more reliable results. In academic settings, the manual review of research manuscripts is a labor-intensive process that requires advisers and panelists to individually examine each section of a submitted document for consistency, and coherence — a task that is both time-consuming and susceptible to human error and subjective judgment. For Resync, Automation Theory justifies the replacement of this manual review process with an AI-powered system capable of automatically comparing submitted documents, detecting inconsistency  between sections, and generating standardized evaluation reports. As the volume of research manuscript submissions in academic institutions continues to grow, automation provides a scalable and objective solution that reduces the burden on academic reviewers while ensuring that students receive consistent and timely feedback on the quality of their research outputs. This shift is critical within regional Philippine higher education institutions, where overextended advisory systems, fragmented institutional resources, and heavy faculty workloads make automated writing evaluation systems necessary to optimize the thesis mentoring cycle (Co, 2025; Trinidad et al., 2025).
In addition to these cognitive and educational frameworks, the proposed system is underpinned by the Semantic Embedding and Semantic Similarity Theory. This framework defines the mathematical and linguistic basis for how artificial intelligence represents and calculates textual meaning. In modern natural language processing, words, sentences, and  paragraphs are projected into high-dimensional vector spaces as dense semantic embeddings (Seo et al., 2025). These mathematical representations allow AI systems to go beyond simple keyword matching and calculate cosine similarity scores between distinct manuscript sections, thereby determining how closely the core concepts correlate (Rokade et al., 2025). For Resync, Semantic Embedding Theory provides the direct algorithm logic used to compare and mathematically score the conceptual coherence between non-contiguous document sections, such as verifying if the stated research objectives in Chapter I correlate with the concluded findings in Chapter V.
Complementing semantic similarity is the Context-Aware Theory, which outlines how an AI system interprets language based on the surrounding structure and operational scope of a document. In academic writing, coherence is defined by the "symmetry of specificity," which dictates that the level of detail, focus, and operational terminology must remain symmetrically balanced across all chapters (Eriksson, 2023). Under Context-Aware Theory, text must be processed as a continuous, structural chain of logical correspondence rather than as isolated sentences (Islamov & Obraztsov, 2026; Plaatjies & Pretorius, 2026). For Resync, this theory justifies the multi-agent parsing architecture that analyzes the document’s global context, ensuring that the operational scope defined in the Title is systematically maintained and addressed in the Problem Statement, Objectives, and Methodology.
These theories underpin the foundational principles of Resync, shaping the development of its features and its intended impact. Information Processing Theory (Miller, 1956; Chikhi et al., 2022) ensures that the system is designed around a structured and logical pipeline for receiving, analyzing, and outputting manuscript evaluation results. Constructivism Theory (Piaget; Vygotsky) strengthens this foundation by addressing the educational purpose of the system's feedback mechanism, ensuring that the generated recommendations actively support student learning and manuscript improvement (Panadero et al., 2023). Automation Theory provides the justification for replacing manual, inconsistent human review with a reliable and scalable AI-powered evaluation process (Co, 2025; Trinidad et al., 2025). Furthermore, Semantic Embedding Theory (Seo et al., 2025; Rokade et al., 2025) and Context-Aware Theory (Eriksson, 2023; Islamov & Obraztsov, 2026) provide the mathematical and structural logic necessary to parse textual meaning and verify cross-section logical flow. By integrating these five theories into its framework, Resync aims to become an academically grounded and technically sound solution that is not only functional and objective but also genuinely supportive of capstone students, advisers, and panelists within Philippine higher education institutions.

manuscript_sections.name: related literature
manuscript_sections.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational settings to perform evaluative tasks and provide structured, criteria-based writing feedback (Seo et al., 2025). Rather than functioning as generic text generators, these models are capable of rating written outputs and checking document coherence with a reasonable degree of consistency under structured, constraint-bound conditions. However, the reliability of these automated judgments depends heavily on the specific evaluation criteria, model selection, and prompt design utilized. This necessitates the development of a highly structured, domain-specific evaluation system that operates under explicit rubrics to generate valid coherence assessments and constructive revision recommendations rather than generic text outputs.
Resync's Coherence Score is computed through a semantic embedding approach rather than direct language-model reasoning. Following the two-stage method demonstrated by Siino (2024) encoding text with the all-mpnet-base-v2 Sentence Transformer and comparing the resulting vectors through cosine similarity  Resync converts each manuscript section into a dense embedding and mathematically measures its semantic correlation with related sections, producing the numerical Coherence Score. This same model-and-method pairing was applied by Siino (2024) to score semantic relatedness between sentence pairs at SemEval-2024, achieving a Spearman correlation of 0.808 for English test data, which supports cosine similarity over MPNet embeddings as a validated method for quantifying textual relatedness at this granularity.
Separately, Google Gemini 2.5 Pro performs the reasoning layer of the system: detecting logical misalignments across sections and generating Explainable AI (XAI) recommendations that justify each flagged inconsistency. This reasoning-based evaluation aligns with the G-Eval framework (Liu et al., 2023), which uses large language models with chain-of-thought prompting and a form-filling paradigm to assess text quality  supporting Gemini's role in explaining detected inconsistencies rather than in generating the Coherence Score itself.
To transition from subjective manuscript evaluation to objective, standardized assessment, systems must analyze text based on a continuous chain of logical correspondence across chapters. Islamov and Obraztsov (2026) developed a 16-step expert-verification algorithm that models academic consistency as a structural network linking key document nodes, tracing the logical flow from the Topic to the Problem, Goal, Tasks, Hypothesis, and Conclusion. By mapping these transitions, this algorithm provides a systematic method to verify that each component directly supports the preceding section, ensuring whole-manuscript integrity. Implementing this verification logic allows Resync to systematically audit the logical flow between a student's research objectives, methodology, and conclusions.
AI systems, particularly large language models, often function as “black boxes,” producing accurate results without clearly explaining how those results were generated. According to Ortigossa et al. (2024), this lack of transparency makes it difficult for users to determine whether an output is reliable or influenced by hidden bias. Explainable AI (XAI) addresses this issue by making AI-generated outputs more understandable. Ortigossa et al. (2024) distinguish interpretability, where a model's reasoning is directly understandable, from explainability, which uses additional methods to clarify why a specific output was produced. This principle is applied in Resync. Instead of presenting only a Coherence Score, the system also provides an Overall Assessment and specific Recommendations that explain detected inconsistencies and suggest improvements. These features make the AI's outputs more transparent and support informed decision-making by researchers, advisers, and panelists.
The integration of automated evaluation rubrics aligns closely with constructivist learning theory, where structured feedback serves as a critical cognitive scaffold to support self-regulated learning. Panadero et al. (2023) demonstrated through a meta-analytic review that rubrics act as evaluative scaffolds that significantly improve academic performance and student self-efficacy, achieving a moderate pooled effect size (g = 0.45). By presenting clear, rubric-driven diagnostic feedback, Resync does not merely edit text but scaffolds the student's writing process within their Zone of Proximal Development. This interaction prompts student researchers to actively reconstruct their research design, facilitating self-regulated learning and deeper cognitive engagement during the revision process.
This automated, scaffolded support is particularly critical in the Philippine educational landscape, where student researchers face severe difficulties maintaining structural consistency and managing the thesis writing lifecycle under overextended advisory systems (Trinidad et al., 2025). Fragmented institutional support, structural time-management issues, and cognitive strain often prevent students from maintaining a logical flow between their research questions and methodologies. These challenges are made worse by manual proofreading and the high number of students assigned to each adviser, causing repeated revisions where errors may only be noticed near the final defense.
The relevance of these writing challenges is especially pronounced when analyzing the bilingual communication patterns of local student researchers. Olitres (2023) investigated the linguistic and academic communication challenges specific to Cebuano-Visayan bilinguals in Philippine educational settings, noting that students frequently encounter writing difficulties when producing academic work in English as a second language. This local context directly influences the types of structural errors and logical inconsistency that occur in draft manuscripts. By addressing these localized academic writing challenges within a unified web application, Resync directly contributes to making capstone evaluation more accessible, structured, and responsive to the regional higher education environment.

manuscript_sections.name: related studies
manuscript_sections.text:
Turnitin is an academic integrity platform used by universities worldwide to check submitted papers against a large database of academic publications and web sources (Turnitin, 2024). The platform compares a submitted document against its repository and produces a similarity report that flags matching or paraphrased text, helping institutions verify originality before a paper is accepted or defended. While effective at detecting copied content, Turnitin does not examine whether a manuscript's internal sections, such as its objectives, problem statement, and conclusions, are logically consistent with one another; its review is limited to textual originality rather than structural or evidentiary coherence.
Similarly, iThenticate, developed by Clarivate Analytics, is widely used in research publishing and academic institutions to ensure originality in scholarly manuscripts. It scans documents against academic journals, publications, and web content to identify potential plagiarism (Clarivate Analytics, n.d.). While it is highly effective in detecting textual overlap, iThenticate does not perform semantic analysis or assess whether the research arguments are structurally consistent across sections of a manuscript.
In terms of writing enhancement, Grammarly is a widely deployed AI-powered writing assistant that provides real-time grammar correction, style improvement, and clarity enhancement (Grammarly Inc., n.d.). It is commonly used by students and professionals to improve writing quality. However, Grammarly operates primarily at the sentence and paragraph level and does not evaluate research-level consistency, such as correlation between research objectives, data analysis, and conclusions.
Beyond grammar-level tools, Paperpal, developed by Editage, is an AI-powered academic writing and manuscript-checking tool used by researchers globally to prepare papers for journal submission (Paperpal, 2024). The tool strengthens a manuscript's structure and flow through AI-generated outlines, contextual recommendations, and consistency checks, and runs over 30 submission-readiness checks covering language, references, structure, and journal compliance before submission. Its consistency-checking feature specifically flags different variations of stylistic elements used throughout a manuscript, identifying where the same term, format, or convention is written inconsistently across sections (Paperpal, 2024). While this shows that an AI tool can already detect internal inconsistencies within a single manuscript, Paperpal's checks focus on accuracy and consistency in numbers, facts, data, symbols, tables, and figures within the document itself rather than comparing the manuscript against separate external documents, such as validation board results or survey data, to verify whether its claims are actually supported by outside evidence.
A more advanced approach to manuscript review is offered by Enago Read (formerly RAxter), an AI-powered peer review platform built around a structured, AI-assisted workspace (Enago Read, 2026). It combines human reviewers with AI-generated insights, using a Copilot interface for querying the manuscript and an LLM Roundtable design to cross-check model outputs and reduce hallucinated feedback. This positions Enago Read as a structured review workspace rather than a simple drafting tool. However, its review still centers on the manuscript as a single document checked against general peer-review checkpoints, not against separate external materials such as validation board results or survey data.
Taken together, these tools reveal a consistent pattern: each one strengthens a different piece of the manuscript review process, originality, grammar, internal stylistic consistency, or peer-review depth, but none of them verifies whether a manuscript's own claims are actually supported by the evidence submitted alongside it. This gap is precisely what Resync is built to close. By checking a research manuscript as a whole against its supporting documents and validating citations against public sources, Resync extends beyond what existing global tools currently offer, addressing a layer of manuscript quality that remains largely unchecked by automated means.

Existing systems such as Turnitin and iThenticate primarily focus on plagiarism detection and similarity checking by comparing submitted documents against academic repositories and online sources. Grammarly and Paperpal, meanwhile, are designed to improve writing quality by offering grammar correction, sentence refinement, and academic writing recommendations. Enago Read supports literature review and document comprehension, but it is limited to single-document analysis and does not evaluate the relationships between different parts of a research manuscript. Although these tools are useful for academic writing support, they do not assess whether the components of a capstone study are logically aligned and consistent as a whole.
Clear differences exist between these systems and the proposed Resync. Unlike existing tools that focus on plagiarism detection, writing enhancement, or literature management, Resync is specifically designed to evaluate the coherence and consistency of capstone manuscript components such as the Statement of the Problem, Objectives of the Study, Survey Results, Validation Board, Scope and Limitations, and other related sections. It determines whether these parts are logically connected and whether each section supports the overall structure of the research study. Resync distinguishes itself by providing a focused approach to manuscript validation centered on structural coherence and logical correlation rather than surface-level writing corrections. By identifying inconsistencies, missing connections, and misaligned components across the research manuscript, the system aims to help students and researchers produce well-structured, consistent, and logically sound capstone studies.

Resync will be developed using the Agile Methodology. This approach is suited to the system, since its core function, using the manuscript template to guide how the AI checks the correlation of content across the manuscript's sections and detect misalignments, requires repeated testing and refinement before it can reliably produce an accurate Coherence Score and Overall Assessment. Developing Resync through short, iterative cycles allows the research team to identify and correct flaws in the comparison process early, rather than discovering them only after the system has been fully built. .
Planning Phase. The team gathers data on the inconsistencies and validation issues encountered by researhers, advisers, and panelists when reviewing research manuscripts and related documents, through surveys and interviews. This data forms the basis of the system's requirements, ensuring that Resync is built around actual review concerns rather than assumptions.
Design Phase. Using the requirements established during planning, the team outlines how Resync will function, including how the system uses the manuscript template to determine the expected content of each section, how it correlates the manuscript's actual content against that expected content to detect misalignments, and how the Coherence Score, Overall Assessment, and Recommendations are presented to the  researcher.
Development Phase. The team implements the design into a working system, developing the features that allow Resync to analyze manuscript content using natural language processing, use the manuscript template to guide the correlation of content across manuscript sections and detect misalignments, validate citations against public sources, and generate recommendations supported by explainable AI. .
Testing Phase. The team verifies that Resync's features function correctly together, ensuring that the system accurately detects misalignments and produces a Coherence Score that reflects an accurate Overall Assessment. Issues identified during testing are corrected before proceeding further.
Deployment Phase. Resync is prepared and released for pilot testing on both web and mobile platforms, with basic guidance provided to help researchers use the system, and with advisers and panelists able to review its output on already pre-checked manuscripts.
Review Phase. The team gathers feedback from pilot users to assess Resync's performance, using their input to identify areas for improvement in future iterations of the system

Experiment 1. Student researchers — Resync's primary users — face persistent difficulty in keeping a capstone or research manuscript correlated and consistent across its title, objectives, methodology, findings, and conclusions, as well as across related documents such as the proposal, manuscript, and defense presentation. Because manuscripts are written over several months and often divided among group members, sections can drift out of sync, and correlations are typically caught only through slow manual re-reading, adviser consultation, or generic grammar-checking tools that do not evaluate the whole manuscript/research. The proposed solution is "Resync," an AI-powered system that automatically compares manuscript sections, computes a Correlation Score reflecting overall correlation, and generates an Inconsistency Report that flags mismatched sections and explains the likely issue. The pilot survey involved 33 respondents — researchers across multiple colleges — gathering feedback on the perceived need for the system and the usefulness of its core features. Success was measured by the proportion of respondents who saw a need for the system and who rated its proposed features as useful. The results — 90.9% affirming the need for the system, 90.9%–93.9% rating its core features as useful, and 93.9% likely or very likely to use or recommend it — validate demand among Resync's primary users and will guide refinement of its detection features ahead of full development.
Experiment 2. Defense panelists, while not primary users of Resync, are nonetheless affected by the same underlying problem: they must manually verify that a capstone manuscript's objectives, methodology, findings, and conclusions remain correlated and internally consistent, often across many defenses per term, using only manual reading, cross-referencing, and general rubrics. As a secondary, optional extension of Resync's core capability, the proposed solution adds a pre-defense readiness that automatically detects misaligned objectives and methodology, checks cross-chapter consistency of terminology, validates completeness, analyzes logical flow between chapters, compares the manuscript against the approved proposal, and checks citation/reference consistency. The pilot key informant interview involved a defense panelist with over 40 capstone defense evaluations across 3–4 years of service, gathering feedback as an affected stakeholder — rather than as a primary user — on the perceived challenge of manual verification, the frequency of post-defense revisions due to correlation issues, and the perceived need for and benefits of an AI-powered readiness report. The results — a "Very Challenging" rating for manual verification, manuscripts "Often" requiring major revisions after a defense, a "Strongly Agree" rating for the system's need, and agreement on all proposed evaluation benefits and checker features — corroborate demand for a panelist-facing readiness report as a secondary module and will guide its prioritization ahead of full development.
Experiment 3. Capstone advisers, likewise not primary users of Resync, experience a parallel — and by this account even more pronounced — version of the same problem as affected stakeholders: repeatedly checking whether a manuscript remains aligned across chapters and revision cycles for every group they advise, relying mainly on manual reading. As a secondary, optional extension of Resync's core capability, the proposed solution adds automatic detection of misaligned objectives and methodology, cross-chapter terminology consistency checking, checklist-based completeness validation, suggested corrective feedback, version comparison to track changes across drafts, and a summary report. The pilot key informant interview involved an adviser with 5 or more years of advising experience and more than 20-40 groups advised in total, gathering feedback as an affected stakeholder — rather than as a primary user — on the perceived challenge of manual verification, the frequency of manuscript inconsistencies and revision cycles required, and the perceived need for and benefits of an AI-powered checker. The results — an "Extremely Challenging" rating for manual verification, manuscripts "Often" showing inconsistencies and typically requiring 3–4 revision cycles, a "Strongly Agree" rating for the system's need, and strong support for corrective-feedback and summary-report features — corroborate demand for an adviser-facing module and will guide its prioritization ahead of full development.

This section refers to the process of creating a detailed data structure for storing, managing, and organizing data in a database management system (DBMS). It involves designing the layout, relationships, and rules that govern how data is stored and accessed within the database.
At the center of the system is the user entity, which extends Supabase's built-in authentication layer and stores basic profile details, including the user's first and last name, email address, and notification preferences. Each user owns one or more manuscript entries, which capture the research paper's title, research type, upload mode, and status. A soft-delete timestamp (deleted_at) allows manuscripts to be archived without permanent data loss.
Every manuscript scan generates an analysis_run, which serves as the central hub of the AI evaluation process. It tracks the scan's status, timestamps, overall coherence score, and an optional style reference URL for dynamic format validation. Each analysis run produces three types of results: inconsistency records, which store the detected issue's type, severity, primary and conflicting section names, Explainable AI (XAI) justifications, suggested fixes, and character offsets for text highlighting in the UI; recommendation records, which capture broader improvement suggestions mapped to specific target sections with an assigned priority level; and citation records, which log the accessibility status of each bibliography reference verified by an asynchronous backend audit.
The subscription entity manages each user's plan tier, AI scan quota limits, and renewal dates to enforce the platform's freemium model. Linked to this is the pymt_txn entity, which serves as a ledger recording each upgrade payment's amount, status, and creation timestamp.
The notification entity stores push alert payloads, OneSignal IDs, and read statuses for in-app delivery, optionally linked to a specific analysis run for deep-link navigation. To support targeted push delivery, the user_device_token entity stores each registered device's OneSignal player ID and platform.
This ERD highlights the interconnected, highly normalized structure of Resync, where user accounts, manuscript submissions, AI analysis results, and subscription management work together to deliver an accurate and explainable manuscript evaluation experience across all platforms.

TECHNOLOGY STACK
"Resync", an AI-powered platform for evaluating research manuscript correlation and inconsistency detection, is developed using a structured and scalable technology stack tailored for academic use in the Philippines. The companion mobile application is built in Android Studio using Kotlin and Jetpack Compose. OneSignal is integrated into the app to deliver real-time, asynchronous push notifications for scan completions.
AI functionalities are powered by a hybrid pipeline of advanced large language models and natural language processing (NLP) libraries. The spaCy library handles the initial manuscript parsing and text tokenization, preparing the data for the Sentence-Transformers framework, which deploys the all-mpnet-base-v2 model to calculate dense vector embeddings and mathematically measure cross-section semantic correlation. For the reasoning layer, Google Gemini 2.5 Pro performs deep semantic analysis to detect logical misalignments and generate Explainable AI (XAI) recommendations.
The backend infrastructure relies on Supabase for robust PostgreSQL relational data handling and secure user authentication. Core backend logic is handled in Python using the FastAPI framework. To facilitate seamless document ingestion without heavy file uploads, the server utilizes the Google Docs API to extract raw text directly from public shareable links. Additionally, the backend deploys Python's httpx library to asynchronously verify external reference URLs for citation validation, ensuring smooth communication between the frontend interfaces, the database, and the external AI layers.
The web component of "Resync", primarily serving as the main workspace for link submission and detailed report analysis, is built with React JS, HTML, Tailwind CSS, and JavaScript/TypeScript. It is deployed via Vercel to ensure highly responsive, dynamic interface delivery and seamless user control over document histories and evaluation reports. Looking ahead, future development includes expanding support to the iOS platform to broaden mobile accessibility and incorporating a Deep Analysis Pro Plan.
